## Pay Per Lead Roofing: How It Works, What It Costs and the Alternative
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/pay-per-lead-roofing

Pay per lead roofing means you pay a vendor a set price for each homeowner contact instead of paying for ads. It is simple and fast to start, but the price per lead is only part of the cost. Whether leads are shared, how they are verified and what you keep when you stop matter just as much.

### What the price per lead does not tell you
- Shared or exclusive: A cheaper lead sent to several roofers can cost more per signed job than an exclusive one.
- Extra fees: Subscriptions, setup or membership fees on top of the per-lead price.
- Refund terms: What counts as a bad lead, and how fast you get a credit or replacement.
- Nothing to keep: When you stop paying, the flow stops and the pages and data stay with the vendor.

### Three ways to pay for roofing leads
- Shared pay per lead: Marketplaces that charge per lead and may send the same homeowner to several pros.
- Exclusive pay per lead: Vendors that sell each lead to one roofer at a higher price per lead.
- Your own system: You pay ad spend and management, and every lead is exclusive to your brand.
- Verified leads for agencies: For pay-per-lead agencies: OTP-verified homeowner leads to resell.

### How does pay per lead roofing work?
A vendor generates homeowner requests through its own ads and websites, then sells each request to one or more roofing companies at a set price. You pay only for the leads you receive, which makes the cost easy to predict, but you do not control how the lead was generated or what the homeowner was promised.

### Roofing lead prices
Prices vary by market, job type and exclusivity. 99 Calls lists exclusive roofing leads at under $50 per lead on its roofing page (99 Calls roofing leads (https://99calls.com/Roofing-Leads.htm)). Google Local Services Ads also charge per lead rather than per click (WebFX on Local Services Ads (https://www.webfx.com/industries/home-repair/roofing/google-local-services-ads)). Across our own published roofing campaigns, cost per lead ranged from $3.75 to $24. Full detail is in how much roofing leads cost (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-much-do-roofing-leads-cost).

### For pay-per-lead agencies
If you sell roofing leads to contractors, lead quality protects your client relationships. For one pay-per-lead agency, every one of 1,024 leads was OTP-verified (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/ppl-agency-1024-otp-verified-roofing-leads) before delivery, at $24 per lead. See lead generation for roofing agencies (https://www.roofingsystems.co/lead-generation-for-roofing-agencies).

### FAQ
Q: What is pay per lead roofing?
A: A model where you pay a vendor a set price for each homeowner request instead of paying for ads yourself. Leads may be shared with other roofers or sold exclusively.
Q: How much do pay per lead roofing leads cost?
A: It varies by market and exclusivity. 99 Calls lists exclusive roofing leads at under $50 per lead. Our own published campaigns ranged from $3.75 to $24 per lead.
Q: Are pay per lead roofing leads exclusive?
A: Some are and some are not. Ask each vendor in writing how many contractors receive every lead.
Q: Is pay per lead cheaper than running my own ads?
A: Not always. Compare cost per signed job. Shared leads can cost more per job, and with your own system you keep the pages, audiences and data.
Q: Do you sell leads per lead?
A: We build and run the lead system for your company, where you pay ad spend and management. We also run campaigns for pay-per-lead agencies that resell verified leads.

### The Dallas roofing market in numbers
Hail is frequent. NOAA's Storm Events Database lists 136 hail reports in Dallas County from 2021 to 2025, 110 of them with hail one inch or larger and the largest at 4 inches. Most came in May, April and March (NOAA Storm Events Database (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/stormevents/)).
Storm losses are large. The same county records list more than $1.3 billion in reported property damage across all storm event types in those five years, including flash flooding as well as hail (NOAA Storm Events Database (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/stormevents/)).
The housing stock is older. About 49.5% of homes in the city of Dallas were built before 1980, and 42.4% of occupied homes are owner-occupied, with a median home value of $295,300 (US Census Bureau, ACS 2019 to 2023 (https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDP5Y2023.DP04?g=160XX00US4819000)).

## Exclusive Roofing Leads for Miami Roofers
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-leads/miami-fl

Miami roofers get exclusive, phone-verified homeowner leads from a city-specific funnel under their own brand. A Florida campaign with separate funnels for Miami, Tampa and Orlando produced 295 verified leads at $22.58 each, and our verified Florida campaigns ran between $19.50 and $22.58 per lead.

### What makes Miami different
- Mostly renters: Only about three in ten occupied homes in the city are owner-occupied, so broad ads reach many people who cannot hire a roofer.
- Condos and multi-family: Many buildings are run by associations and property managers, which is a commercial sale, not a homeowner sale.
- A long storm season: The Atlantic hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November.
- Fake and wrong numbers: Unverified forms waste calls; verification matters more in a crowded market.

### How we run roofing campaigns in Miami
- A Miami-only funnel: A page and campaign for Miami alone, run side by side with other Florida cities.
- OTP verification: Every lead confirms a one-time code before it reaches your team.
- Owner-occupied targeting: Targeting and qualifying questions that focus on homeowners, not renters.
- Bilingual campaigns: Ads and follow-up in English and Spanish when your team serves both.

### The Miami roofing market in numbers
Owners are a minority. Only about 30.7% of occupied homes in the city of Miami are owner-occupied, and about 23.1% of housing units are single-family detached homes (US Census Bureau, ACS 2019 to 2023 (https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDP5Y2023.DP04?g=160XX00US1245000)).
The housing stock is old and valuable. About 52.4% of Miami's homes were built before 1980, and the median value of owner-occupied homes is $475,200 (US Census Bureau, ACS 2019 to 2023 (https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDP5Y2023.DP04?g=160XX00US1245000)).
Storms beyond hurricanes. NOAA's Storm Events Database lists 43 thunderstorm wind reports, 23 hail reports and 7 tornadoes in Miami-Dade County from 2021 to 2025, with hail most often in April and May (NOAA Storm Events Database (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/stormevents/)).

With many multi-family buildings, a share of Miami roofing work is decided by associations and property managers. That is a longer, commercial sale with several decision makers. See commercial roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/commercial-roofing-leads) for how we approach it.

## Roofing Lead Cost Report 2026: What 18 Campaigns and 11,190 Leads Cost
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-lead-cost-report-2026

Short answer: Across 18 published roofing campaigns and 11,190 leads, cost per lead ranged from $3.75 to $24, with a median of $13.40. Phone-verified campaigns had a median of $14.80 per lead; standard campaigns had a median of $5.31. Verification adds cost per lead but removes fake and unreachable numbers.

This report pulls together every published roofing campaign on this site that lists a cost per lead: 18 campaigns and 11,190 leads, run on Facebook and Instagram between August 2025 and October 2026. Client names are left out. Each figure links to its full case study.

### Headline numbers
All 18 published campaigns with a cost per lead.
Measure | Value | Notes
Campaigns | 18 | Every published case study on this site that lists a cost per lead
Leads | 11,190 | Sum of the lead counts in those case studies
Median cost per lead | $13.40 | Half the campaigns were below, half above
Lowest | $3.75 | 25 leads on a campaign's first day (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/roofing-25-leads-one-day-3-75)
Highest | $24 | 1,024 OTP-verified leads for a pay-per-lead agency (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/ppl-agency-1024-otp-verified-roofing-leads)

### How much do roofing leads cost?
In our published campaigns, between $3.75 and $24 per lead, with a median of $13.40. Where a campaign falls in that range depends mostly on the offer, the creative, the market and how strictly leads are verified. Cost per lead is only the first number: what matters is cost per booked inspection and cost per signed job.

### Verified vs standard leads
Campaigns whose case study describes leads as verified, OTP-verified or validated, compared with the rest.
Group | Campaigns | Median cost per lead
Phone-verified or validated | 9 | $14.80
Standard | 9 | $5.31
Verification adds a step for the homeowner, so fewer people finish the form and each lead costs more. In exchange, numbers are real and reachable before your team calls. For many roofing companies the higher cost per lead is offset by fewer wasted calls. See verified roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/verified-roofing-leads).

### Texas and Florida
The two Texas campaigns in the report came in at $5.31 and $7.60 per lead; neither case study describes its leads as verified. The two Florida roofing campaigns, at $19.50 and $22.58, used OTP verification across several locations. With only two campaigns per state, the difference says more about verification than about the state itself. Market detail is on roofing leads in Texas (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-leads-texas) and roofing leads in Florida (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-leads-florida).

### What drives roofing cost per lead
- The offer. A specific offer, such as $0-down financing, took one Texas roofer from zero leads to 686 in 8 days at $5.31.
- Creative. Most of the lowest-cost campaigns held a click-through rate above 2%; the Texas 850-lead campaign reached 3.79%.
- Verification. OTP and multi-step validation raise cost per lead and lower the share of bad numbers.
- Scale and time. Long-running campaigns, such as 1,480 leads at $4.77 over five months, keep cost per lead low with clear rules for launching, killing and scaling ads.

### Method and limits
Included: every case study on roofingsystems.co that states a single cost per lead, as published on 25 November 2026. Excluded: case studies without a cost per lead, ranges instead of a single figure, and the Florida home service campaign that also covered gutters and solar. Campaigns differ in market, offer, budget and length, so treat these numbers as real benchmarks, not a quote for your market. An earlier study of 15 of these campaigns is in roofing Facebook ads cost per lead (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-facebook-ads-cost-per-lead).
You may cite this report with a link to this page. For what leads would cost in your area, see how much roofing leads cost (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-much-do-roofing-leads-cost) or book a free strategy call (https://www.roofingsystems.co/book).

## What Do Roofing Facebook Ads Cost Per Lead? Data From 15 Real Campaigns
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-facebook-ads-cost-per-lead

Short answer: Across 15 roofing Meta ad campaigns and 7,765 homeowner leads, the median cost per lead was $11.41, ranging from $3.75 to $24. Commonly cited industry benchmarks put roofing Facebook leads at roughly $40 to $80. Cost per lead is only a starting point: what matters is cost per booked inspection and per signed job.

Most published numbers on roofing Facebook ad costs are broad industry benchmarks. Here are the actual cost-per-lead results from 15 roofing campaigns we ran on Meta (Facebook and Instagram) between September 2025 and October 2026, with each campaign linked to its case study so you can check the numbers.

### The headline numbers
- 15 campaigns, 7,765 leads for roofing contractors and one roofing pay-per-lead agency.
- Median cost per lead: $11.41. Lowest $3.75 (day one of a campaign), highest $24.
- 13 of 15 campaigns came in under $15 per lead, and 7 of 15 under $10.
- Blended CPL $11.98 across the 9 campaigns that also reported total spend ($50,853 spent, 4,244 leads).
For comparison, published roofing benchmarks commonly cluster around $40 to $80 per lead on Facebook (see the WebTonic roofing Meta ads statistics report (https://www.webtonic.io/blog/roofing-facebook-ads-statistics) and JobNimbus on when Facebook ads work for roofers (https://jobnimbus.com/blog/why-facebook-ads-fail-roofers-and-when-they-actually-work)). Those are averages across very different accounts, so treat the gap as a sign of what a structured system can do, not a promise.

### Campaign-by-campaign data
Cost per lead by campaign (newest first). Each campaign links to its case study.
Campaign | Leads | Cost per lead | Notes
Roofing companies, Oct 2026 (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/roofing-201-leads-14-45-cpl) | 201 | $14.45 | First days after launch
Florida & Bay Area, day one (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/roofing-25-leads-one-day-3-75) | 25 | $3.75 | $93 spend, single day
Roofing client, 28 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/roofing-227-leads-14-cpl-28-days) | 227 | $14 | Verified leads, CTR above 2%

Brand-new ad account, 7 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/261-otp-verified-leads-7-days-new-account) | 261 | $14.80 | OTP-verified, no pixel history
Florida, 4 locations, 16 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/florida-365-otp-verified-leads-4-locations) | 365 | $19.50 | OTP-verified, CRM follow-up
One roofing client, Oct–Feb (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/1480-roofing-leads-4-77-cpl) | 1,480 | $4.77 | $26.77 CPM

US roofer, Oct 25–Nov 27 (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/825-verified-roofing-leads-4-95-cpl) | 825 | $4.95 | $1.33 CPC, $24 CPM
Texas roofer, 8 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/texas-roofer-686-leads-8-days-0-down-offer) | 686 | $5.31 | $0-down financing offer, 2.17% CTR
New client, first 13 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/537-qualified-leads-13-days-andromeda-update) | 537 | $4.27 | TX, FL & GA jobs
Pay-per-lead agency (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/ppl-agency-1024-otp-verified-roofing-leads) | 1,024 | $24 | OTP-verified, 1.63% CTR
Texas roofer, 8 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/texas-850-roofing-leads-8-days-7-60) | 850 | $7.60 | 3.79% CTR
*Calculated from the campaign's reported spend ($3,196) divided by leads (280). For the 45-day campaign reported as $4–$6, the median uses the $5 midpoint.

### What the lowest-CPL campaigns had in common
Reading across the case studies, the same few factors come up again and again:
1. A specific offer, not "free inspection". The Texas roofer that went from zero leads to 686 in 8 days switched to a $0-down, 0%-interest-for-12-months financing offer. (Financing claims need the lender's terms and the required disclosures.)
2. Creative that earns the click. Most low-CPL campaigns held a click-through rate above 2%, and one reached 3.79%. A higher CTR usually means cheaper leads on Meta.
3. Targeting built around intent. Audience segmentation and intent layering instead of one broad audience. We cover this in the free audience segmentation training (https://www.roofingsystems.co/privatemastermind).
4. Lead verification. Several campaigns used OTP (one-time passcode) verification, so every counted lead had a real, reachable phone number. Verified leads usually cost a little more but waste less sales time.
5. Speed. Campaigns were launched and adjusted fast; the brand-new account with no pixel history still reached $14.80 per lead in its first week.

### Why cost per lead is not the number to optimize
A $5 lead that never answers the phone is more expensive than a $20 lead that books an inspection. The figure that pays the bills is cost per signed job. In the clearest example we have, a Dallas roofer turned its campaign into $127,500 in closed deals and 34 installs in about 60 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/dallas-roofer-127500-closed-34-installs). That outcome depended as much on fast follow-up (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-lead-follow-up) and qualification as on the ad cost.
Definitions: Cost per lead (CPL): ad spend divided by the number of leads. OTP-verified lead: a lead who confirmed their phone number with a one-time passcode. CTR: the share of people who saw the ad and clicked it. CPM: the cost of 1,000 ad impressions.

### How to read this data
- These are our own campaigns, reported in the original posts; we have not mixed in third-party data.
- 15 campaigns is a small sample, and markets, offers and seasons differ. Your results will differ too: see our income disclosure (https://www.roofingsystems.co/income-disclosure).
- Lead definitions vary: some campaigns count form fills, others only OTP-verified or pre-qualified leads.
- Most campaigns report results from the first days or weeks; costs can rise or fall as campaigns mature.
Want to see how these numbers were produced? Read about Facebook ads for roofers (https://www.roofingsystems.co/facebook-ads-for-roofers), the full roofing lead generation system (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-lead-generation), or browse all case studies (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies).

### FAQ
Q: What is a good cost per lead for roofing Facebook ads?
A: Across our 15 roofing Meta campaigns the median was $11.41 per lead, and 13 of 15 were under $15. Industry benchmarks commonly cited for roofing Facebook leads are around $40 to $80. A good CPL is one that turns into booked inspections and signed jobs at a profitable cost.
Q: Why are some roofing leads so much cheaper than others?
A: In our campaigns the lowest costs came with a specific offer (such as $0-down financing), creative with a click-through rate above 2%, intent-based audience targeting and fast launch and iteration.
Q: Are cheap roofing leads lower quality?
A: Not necessarily, but cheap leads can be unqualified. Verification (such as OTP phone verification), qualification questions and fast follow-up decide whether low-cost leads turn into appointments.
Q: Is cost per lead the best way to measure roofing ads?
A: No. Cost per lead is a starting point; cost per booked inspection and cost per signed job show whether the ads are profitable.

## How Much Do Roofing Leads Cost? 2026 Prices by Source
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-much-do-roofing-leads-cost

Short answer: Roofing leads typically cost $4 to $25 each from your own Facebook and Instagram ads (median $11.41 across our 15 roofing campaigns), around $55 each from exclusive pay-per-lead vendors, and $18 to $42 per click on Google before a single form is filled. The number that matters most is cost per signed job.

Roofing lead prices vary more by source than by market. Here is what each source costs, using our own campaign data, Semrush click prices and published vendor prices, with links so you can check every number.

### Roofing lead cost by source
Typical roofing lead costs by source. Sources linked in the text below.
Source | Typical cost | Exclusive? | Notes

Google Ads | $18–$42 per click | Yes | Semrush CPC, Nov 2026; cost per lead is higher than per click

### Facebook and Instagram ads
Across 15 of our roofing campaigns on Meta, cost per lead ranged from $3.75 to $24 with a median of $11.41. Semrush data from November 2026 puts the average cost per click at $22.36 for "roofing leads", $42.46 for "roofing leads texas" and $18.77 for "google ads for roofers". Only some clicks become leads, so cost per lead on Google is usually several times the click price. More in Google Ads for roofers (https://www.roofingsystems.co/google-ads-for-roofers).

### Pay-per-lead vendors
Exclusive pay-per-lead vendors publish prices around $55 per lead (for example, 99 Calls Texas roofing leads (https://99calls.com/locations/Texas/Roofing-Leads.htm)). Shared leads are cheaper per lead but go to several contractors at once. See shared vs exclusive roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/shared-vs-exclusive-roofing-leads).

### Cost per signed job matters more
A cheap lead that never answers costs more than an expensive one that books. Track cost per inspection and per signed job. In our Dallas campaign (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/dallas-roofer-127500-closed-34-installs), the result that mattered was $127,500 closed and 34 installs in about 60 days. Phone verification (https://www.roofingsystems.co/verified-roofing-leads) and fast follow-up (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-lead-follow-up) are what turn cheap leads into jobs.
Lowering your cost per lead: Use a specific offer, real job creative, verified forms and instant follow-up. We build all four as one system: exclusive roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/).

### FAQ
Q: How much does a roofing lead cost?
A: From your own Facebook and Instagram ads, typically $4 to $25 (median $11.41 across our 15 roofing campaigns). Exclusive pay-per-lead vendors publish prices around $55. Google clicks alone cost $18 to $42.
Q: Are cheaper roofing leads worse?
A: Not necessarily. Cheap leads can be unqualified, but verification, qualifying questions and fast follow-up decide whether they turn into inspections.
Q: Why are roofing leads more expensive in Texas?
A: Competition. Semrush shows a $42.46 cost per click for "roofing leads texas", about double the national figure for "roofing leads". Our own Texas Meta campaigns still came in at $5.31 and $7.60 per lead.
Q: Are roofing leads worth it?
A: They are worth it when your cost per signed job stays well below the profit on a roof. Work it out as cost per lead divided by your close rate. For scale, a Dallas roofer in our case studies closed $127,500 from 34 installs, about $3,750 per job, so the cost to win each job has to stay well under that.
Q: How much do shared vs exclusive roofing leads cost?
A: Exclusive pay-per-lead vendors publish prices around $55 per lead. Shared leads cost less per lead but go to several roofers at once. Leads from your own Facebook and Instagram ads cost $3.75 to $24 in our 15 roofing campaigns, with a median of $11.41, and are exclusive to you.
Q: What is the average cost of a roofing lead in 2026?
A: Across 18 published roofing campaigns and 11,190 leads from Roofing Systems Co., the median cost per lead was $13.40, with a range of $3.75 to $24. Phone-verified campaigns had a median of $14.80 and standard campaigns $5.31. The full data is in the Roofing Lead Cost Report 2026.
Q: What is a good cost per lead for roofing?
A: One that produces booked inspections and signed jobs at a profit. As a benchmark, our 15 roofing Meta campaigns had a median of $11.41 per lead.

## How to Choose a Roofing Lead Generation Company: 10 Questions to Ask
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-to-choose-a-roofing-lead-generation-company

Short answer: Choose a roofing lead generation company that gives you exclusive leads, verifies phone numbers, lets you own the pages and data, shows real campaign numbers, measures cost per signed job and doesn't lock you into a long contract.

Roofing lead generation companies range from lead sellers to full-service agencies. Some are excellent; some resell the same homeowner to five roofers. These 10 questions separate them quickly.

### The four types of roofing lead generation companies
- Shared lead sellers: sell each homeowner to several roofers. Cheap per lead, high competition per lead.
- Exclusive pay-per-lead vendors: one roofer per lead, priced per lead (around $55 in published Texas prices). You still rent the leads.
- Marketing agencies: run ads in your name. Quality depends on whether they also handle pages, follow-up and qualification.
- System builders: build ads, pages, CRM and follow-up you own. More setup, but the assets keep working. This is what we do: roofing lead generation (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-lead-generation).

### 10 questions to ask before you sign
1. Are the leads exclusive to my company? If not, you are competing on every call. See shared vs exclusive (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/shared-vs-exclusive-roofing-leads).
2. How do you verify leads? Look for phone verification (OTP) and qualifying questions: verified roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/verified-roofing-leads).
3. Who owns the ads, landing pages and customer data? If you leave, what stays with you?
4. Can you show real roofing campaign numbers? Ask for cost per lead, lead volume and ideally closed revenue. Ours are public: case studies (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies).
5. What does a lead cost, and what does a signed job cost? Cost per job is the real number. Benchmarks in how much roofing leads cost (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-much-do-roofing-leads-cost).
6. How fast is the first contact? Leads should get a text and email within minutes: lead follow-up (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-lead-follow-up).
7. What offer and creative will you run? A specific offer beats "free inspection": roofing ads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-ad-creatives).
8. Do you work in my market? Ask for results near you, for example Texas (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-leads-texas) or Florida (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-leads-florida).
9. How long is the contract? Prefer written performance terms over long lock-ins.
10. What do the weekly reports show? Inspections and jobs, not just clicks and impressions.

### Red flags
- No real numbers, only testimonials.
- Leads delivered by spreadsheet or email with no CRM.
- Unclear whether leads are shared.
- Guarantees of a number of jobs (nobody controls whether homeowners buy).
How we answer these questions: Exclusive leads under your brand, OTP verification, assets you own, public case studies and a 90-day written agreement. See exclusive roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/) or the full list of services (https://www.roofingsystems.co/services).

### FAQ
Q: What is the best roofing lead generation company?
A: The best one for you gives exclusive, verified leads, lets you own the assets, shows real campaign numbers and measures cost per signed job. Use the 10 questions above to compare.
Q: Which roofing lead generation companies should I compare?
A: Compare four types: shared marketplaces such as Angi, HomeAdvisor and Thumbtack; exclusive lead vendors such as 99 Calls; Google Local Services Ads; and owned systems such as Roofing Systems Co. Judge each by exclusivity, verification, total cost, published results and who owns the data.
Q: Should I buy leads or build my own system?
A: Buying leads is faster to start; an owned system costs more effort up front but keeps working and the leads are exclusive. Many roofers start with one and move to the other.
Q: How much do roofing lead generation companies charge?
A: Pay-per-lead vendors price per lead (around $55 in published Texas prices); agencies usually charge a management fee plus ad spend. Our own Meta campaigns had a median ad cost of $11.41 per lead.

## How to Get Roofing Leads: 9 Free and Paid Ways, Compared
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-to-get-roofing-leads

Short answer: The best way to get roofing leads is to combine free sources (Google Business Profile, reviews, referrals and job-site marketing) with one paid channel you control, such as Meta ads under your own brand. Across 15 of our roofing Meta campaigns, the median cost per lead was $11.41.

There is no single best way to get roofing leads. Free methods build trust but grow slowly; paid methods are fast but cost money every month. Here are the nine methods roofing companies use, what each one costs, and how to combine them.

### Free ways to get roofing leads
Free roofing leads cost time instead of money. They are slower, but they build the reviews and reputation that make every paid channel cheaper.
1. Google Business Profile. Complete every field, add real job photos weekly and answer every review. It is the free listing that shows in Google Maps for "roofer near me" searches.
2. Reviews. Ask every happy customer for a Google review the day the job finishes. Reviews feed your Maps ranking and your ads: in our Dallas campaign (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/dallas-roofer-127500-closed-34-installs), ads built around existing reviews led to $127,500 closed.
3. Referrals. Give past customers a simple reason and a simple way to refer neighbors, such as a referral card left at handover.
4. Job-site marketing. Yard signs and door hangers on the streets around each job reach neighbors who just watched your crew work.
5. Community groups. Helpful answers in local Facebook groups and Nextdoor build recognition. Don't spam: share advice and photos.

### Paid ways to get roofing leads
1. Meta ads (Facebook and Instagram). Reach homeowners before they search, with an offer and creative you control. Our roofing campaigns ranged from $3.75 to $24 per lead; see the cost per lead study (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-facebook-ads-cost-per-lead).
2. Google Ads and Local Services Ads. Catch people already searching. Higher intent, higher cost: advertisers pay around $18–$22 per click for roofing lead keywords (Semrush, November 2026). More in Google Ads for roofers (https://www.roofingsystems.co/google-ads-for-roofers).
3. Buying leads. Fast, but leads are often shared with other contractors and stop when you stop paying. Compare options in shared vs exclusive roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/shared-vs-exclusive-roofing-leads).
4. Your own lead generation system. Ads, landing pages, CRM and follow-up you own, so the assets keep working. This is what we build: roofing lead generation (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-lead-generation).

### How to get roofing leads on Facebook
Facebook (and Instagram) leads come from paid Meta ads, not from posting on your page. The roofers in our case studies who got the cheapest leads followed the same four steps:
1. Run a lead campaign, not a boosted post. Boosts optimise for likes; lead campaigns optimise for homeowners who fill in a form.
2. Lead with a specific offer. A $0-down financing offer produced 686 homeowner leads in 8 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/texas-roofer-686-leads-8-days-0-down-offer) for a Texas roofer.
3. Use real job photos and video. Creative is what keeps click-through rates above 2% and cost per lead down.
4. Verify and follow up instantly. Phone verification and an automatic text and email within minutes turn leads into inspections.
Across 15 of our roofing Meta campaigns, the median cost per lead was $11.41 (full study (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-facebook-ads-cost-per-lead)). See how the system works in roofing Facebook ads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/facebook-ads-for-roofers) and Instagram ads for roofers (https://www.roofingsystems.co/instagram-ads-for-roofers).

### Which method is the best way to get roofing leads?
Roofing lead sources compared. Costs are typical ranges; your market will differ.
Method | Cost | Speed | Exclusive?
Google Business Profile and reviews | Free (time) | Slow | Yes
Referrals and job-site marketing | Low | Slow | Yes
Community groups | Free (time) | Slow | Yes
Meta ads under your brand | Ad spend; our median $11.41 per lead | Fast | Yes
Google Ads / Local Services Ads | High cost per click | Fast | Yes
Bought leads | Per lead, ongoing | Fast | Often shared
For most $1M+ roofing companies, the best mix is free sources for trust plus one paid channel you own for predictable volume. Whatever the source, follow-up decides whether a lead becomes a job (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-lead-follow-up).
Don't forget follow-up: The cheapest roofing lead is the one you already paid for. Respond within minutes, verify the number and keep following up. See roofing CRM automation (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-crm-automation).

### FAQ
Q: How do I get free roofing leads?
A: Through your Google Business Profile, reviews, referrals, yard signs and door hangers around jobs, and helpful posts in local community groups. They take time but cost little.
Q: What is the best way to get roofing leads?
A: Combine free sources that build trust with one paid channel you control. For many roofers that is Meta ads under their own brand; our 15 roofing campaigns had a median cost per lead of $11.41.
Q: How do I get roofing leads on Facebook?
A: Run a Meta lead campaign (not a boosted post) with a specific offer, real job photos or video, phone verification and instant follow-up. Across 15 of our roofing campaigns the median cost per lead was $11.41.
Q: Should I buy roofing leads?
A: Bought leads are fast but often shared with other roofers and stop when you stop paying. An owned system costs more effort up front but keeps working.
Q: How fast can I get roofing leads?
A: Paid ads can produce leads within days; one of our campaigns produced 25 leads on its first day. Free methods take weeks to months.

## Digital Marketing for Roofing Companies: What Works in 2026
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/digital-marketing-for-roofing-companies

Short answer: Digital marketing for roofing companies works best as one system: paid social or search ads that reach homeowners in your area, a landing page that matches the ad, phone verification, instant follow-up and a CRM that tracks every lead to a signed job. Reviews and a strong Google Business Profile support it.

Roofers hear a lot of advice about digital marketing. This guide compares the channels that actually bring roofing leads, what each one costs, and how to tell whether it is working, using numbers from roofing campaigns we have run.

### What digital marketing for roofers includes
- Google Business Profile and reviews. The listing homeowners see in Google Maps. Free, slow to build, and a trust signal for everything else.
- Website and landing pages. Your website explains the company; roofing landing pages (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-landing-pages) turn ad clicks into booked inspections.
- Paid social (Facebook and Instagram). Reaches homeowners before they search, with offers and video from your real jobs.
- Search ads. Google Ads and Local Services Ads catch people already searching for a roofer, at a higher cost per click.
- Follow-up and CRM. Instant text and email, reminders and a pipeline from first click to signed contract.
- Email and SMS to past customers and estimates. Reviews, referrals and old estimates that can still turn into jobs.

### Roofing marketing channels compared
Typical costs by channel. Meta figures are from our 15 roofing campaigns; Google and vendor figures are cited in our cost guide.
Channel | Best for | Speed | Typical cost
Facebook and Instagram ads | Steady homeowner leads, replacement and financing offers | Days | $3.75 to $24 per lead (median $11.41)
Google Ads | Urgent repair and replacement searches | Days | $18 to $42 per click
Exclusive pay-per-lead vendors | Quick volume without running ads | Days | Around $55 per lead
Google Business Profile and reviews | Local trust and map listings | Months | Free (time)
Referrals and past customers | High-trust jobs | Ongoing | Free (time)
Sources and detail for every figure are in how much roofing leads cost (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-much-do-roofing-leads-cost) and our cost per lead study across 15 roofing campaigns (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-facebook-ads-cost-per-lead).

### Paid social: where most of our roofing leads come from
Facebook and Instagram reach homeowners before they start comparing roofers, so the offer and the creative do the selling. Campaigns we have run produced 1,480 roofing leads at $4.77 each (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/1480-roofing-leads-4-77-cpl) over five months and 686 leads in 8 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/texas-roofer-686-leads-8-days-0-down-offer) for a Texas roofer with a $0-down financing offer. See how the system is built in Facebook ads for roofers (https://www.roofingsystems.co/facebook-ads-for-roofers).

### Search: Google Business Profile and Google Ads
Search catches homeowners who already need a roofer. A complete Google Business Profile with photos and recent reviews costs nothing but time. Google Ads and Local Services Ads cost more per click and are capped by how many people search, so they work best for urgent repairs. Our Google Ads for roofers (https://www.roofingsystems.co/google-ads-for-roofers) guide covers campaign types and costs.

### Your website and landing pages
A roofing website builds trust and supports search. Paid traffic converts better on a landing page with one offer, proof near the form, tap-to-call and a short qualifying form. Pages like these powered 850 leads in 8 days at $7.60 (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/texas-850-roofing-leads-8-days-7-60) for a Texas roofer.

### Follow-up and CRM: where the money is made
Most roofing leads are lost after they come in. An instant reply, reminders and a CRM that tracks each lead to a signed job turn the same ad spend into more revenue. For a Florida roofing company, the CRM showed $111,200 in won revenue in 31 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/florida-roofer-111k-31-days). See roofing CRM automation (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-crm-automation).

### How to measure roofing digital marketing
1. Cost per lead. Useful for comparing ads, but never the whole story.
2. Contact rate. How many leads your team actually reaches. Phone verification raises it.
3. Cost per booked inspection. The first number that shows real demand.
4. Cost per signed job. The number that decides whether marketing pays.
5. Revenue by source. Which channel, ad and page produced the jobs, tracked in your CRM.

### Choosing a digital marketing agency for roofers
Ask who owns the ad account and the data, whether leads are exclusive, which real roofing results the agency can show with numbers, how fast leads are contacted and what is reported each week. Our full checklist is in how to choose a roofing lead generation company (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-to-choose-a-roofing-lead-generation-company). We work as a roofing marketing agency (https://www.roofingsystems.co/) for companies doing $1M+ a year; see our approach to roofing contractor marketing (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-marketing).

### FAQ
Q: What is digital marketing for roofing companies?
A: Using online channels to win roofing jobs: Google Business Profile and reviews, a website and landing pages, Facebook, Instagram and Google ads, and follow-up through a CRM, text and email. It works best when these parts are connected as one system.
Q: What is the best digital marketing for roofers?
A: The one that produces signed jobs at a profit in your market. For most $1M+ roofing companies that means paid social for steady homeowner leads, search for urgent repairs, a matching landing page and fast follow-up.
Q: How much does digital marketing cost for a roofing company?
A: It depends on your market and budget. In our 15 roofing campaigns on Facebook and Instagram, cost per lead ranged from $3.75 to $24, with a median of $11.41. Google Ads clicks for roofing searches cost around $18 to $42.
Q: Is Facebook or Google better for roofing companies?
A: Google catches people already searching, while Facebook reaches homeowners earlier and often at a lower cost per lead. Many roofing companies use both: Facebook for volume and Google for urgent repairs.
Q: How do I know if my roofing marketing is working?
A: Track cost per booked inspection and cost per signed job, not just cost per lead, and tag every lead with its source in your CRM so you can see which channel produced the revenue.

## Roofing Marketing in the Off-Season: How to Keep Leads Coming
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-marketing-off-season

Short answer: To get roofing leads in the off-season, shift from storm messaging to replacement and financing offers, contact old estimates and past customers, ask for reviews and referrals, and keep fast follow-up running. Campaigns we ran from October to February produced over 1,400 leads each at around $5 per lead.

When the weather is quiet, many roofing calendars go quiet too. It does not have to happen: some of our strongest roofing campaigns ran between October and February. Here is what works when there is no storm to ride.

### Why roofing leads slow down between storms
Many roofing companies depend on storms, referrals and door knocking. When the weather is quiet, demand from storm damage drops, but homeowners with ageing roofs still plan replacements, sell homes and compare quotes. The work is still there; the message has to change.

### What worked between October and February
Published roofing campaigns that ran in the off-season.
Campaign | Period | Result
1,865 roofing leads at $5.24 (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/1865-roofing-leads-5-24-cpl-oct-jan) | 18 Oct 2025 to 14 Jan 2026 | 1,865 leads, $9,770 spent
1,480 roofing leads at $4.77 (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/1480-roofing-leads-4-77-cpl) | October to February | 1,480 leads at $4.77 each
Dallas roofer, $127,500 closed (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/dallas-roofer-127500-closed-34-installs) | 18 Dec to 19 Feb | $18,000 in late December, $75,600 in January, $33,900 in February; 34 installs

### 7 ways to get roofing leads in the off-season
1. Lead with replacement and financing offers. A clear payment option answers the biggest objection to a new roof. A $0-down, 0%-for-12-months offer produced 686 leads in 8 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/texas-roofer-686-leads-8-days-0-down-offer) for a Texas roofer, with no storm involved. See roof replacement leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roof-replacement-leads).
2. Contact old estimates. Homeowners who got a quote and never signed are the warmest list you have. A seasonal message or offer costs nothing in ad spend.
3. Ask for reviews and referrals. Quiet weeks are the time to ask every recent customer for a Google review and a referral.
4. Retarget past visitors. People who visited your site or landing page in storm season can be reminded with financing and warranty ads.
5. Sell pre-season inspections. Before hail season or the hurricane season, offer inspections to homeowners who want to be ready.
6. Keep follow-up running. Off-season leads take longer to decide, so text and email sequences matter even more. See roofing CRM automation (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-crm-automation).
7. Add commercial maintenance. Property managers plan roof work and budgets year-round. See commercial roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/commercial-roofing-leads).

### Should you cut your ad budget in winter?
Not automatically. Fewer roofers advertise in quiet months, so a campaign with a strong replacement offer can keep cost per lead low, as the October to February campaigns above show. Judge it on cost per booked inspection and per signed job, and pause only when your crews are full. For budgeting, see how much roofing leads cost (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-much-do-roofing-leads-cost).

### Use the quiet months to get storm-ready
The off-season is also the time to prepare: creative from this year's jobs, landing pages for each area you serve, and a CRM that can respond in minutes. When the next storm hits, the campaign is ready to launch the same day. See storm damage leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/storm-damage-leads) and the full roofing lead generation (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-lead-generation) system.

### FAQ
Q: How do roofers get leads in the off-season?
A: By switching from storm messaging to replacement and financing offers, contacting old estimates and past customers, asking for reviews and referrals, retargeting past visitors and keeping fast follow-up running.
Q: Do roofing ads work in winter?
A: Yes. Some of our strongest roofing campaigns ran in the off-season: 1,865 leads at $5.24 from October to January, and 1,480 leads at $4.77 from October to February.
Q: Should roofers stop advertising when it is slow?
A: Not automatically. Fewer competitors advertise in quiet months, so a strong replacement offer can keep costs low. Pause only when your crews are fully booked.
Q: What is the best offer for off-season roofing leads?
A: A replacement offer that answers the cost objection, such as financing. A $0-down, 0%-for-12-months offer produced 686 leads in 8 days for a Texas roofer. Financing offers need the lender's terms and disclosures.
Q: Can a roofer close jobs in December and January?
A: Yes. A Dallas roofer in our case studies closed $18,000 in the last two weeks of December and $75,600 in January, part of $127,500 and 34 installs in about 60 days.

## How to Start a Roofing Company: 10 Steps From License to First Jobs
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-to-start-a-roofing-company

Short answer: To start a roofing company, choose your niche and market, form the business, get the contractor license your state requires, buy general liability and workers compensation insurance, set prices from your real costs, line up a crew and suppliers, build a simple website and Google Business Profile, and set up a way to get roofing leads before your first job ends.

Starting a roofing company takes more than knowing how to roof. You need the right licenses and insurance, prices that cover your real costs, a crew and suppliers you can count on, and a steady way to find homeowners who need work. This guide walks through each step in order.

### How to start a roofing company in 10 steps
1. Pick your niche and market. Residential replacement, repair, storm work or commercial roofing each need different crews, equipment and sales skills. Start with one.
2. Write a simple business plan. Your service area, target jobs, startup costs, prices and how you will find customers.
3. Form the business. Register the company, get a tax ID and open a business bank account.
4. Get licensed. Roofing license rules differ by state and sometimes by city. Check your state's contractor licensing board before you take any job.
5. Get insured. General liability and workers compensation are the basics most homeowners, general contractors and suppliers will ask about. Ask a commercial insurance agent what your state and your jobs require.
6. Set your prices from real costs. Materials, labor, disposal, permits, insurance, vehicles, overhead and the profit you need on every job.
7. Line up suppliers and crews. Open accounts with local roofing suppliers and decide between employees and subcontractors.
8. Get the right tools and vehicle. Safety equipment first, then what your first jobs actually need.
9. Build your online presence. A simple website, a complete Google Business Profile with real job photos, and a way to collect reviews after every job.
10. Set up a lead system. Referrals alone rarely fill a calendar. Plan how you will get roofing leads every month.

### What it costs to start
Costs depend on your state, whether you buy or lease a vehicle and equipment, insurance premiums and how much marketing you do in the first months. Build a budget that covers several months of overhead before revenue arrives, because roofing jobs are often paid on completion and insurance-related work can take longer to pay.

### How to get your first roofing customers
- Friends, family and past employers. Your first jobs often come from people who already trust you. Do them well and ask for a review and a referral.
- Google Business Profile. Free, and the first thing many homeowners check. Add real photos of every job.
- Local partners. Real estate agents, property managers and home inspectors see roofs that need work.
- Paid ads. Facebook and Instagram ads reach homeowners in your area before they search. Our published roofing campaigns ranged from $3.75 to $24 per lead. See how to get roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-to-get-roofing-leads).

### Mistakes that sink new roofing companies
- Pricing jobs to win instead of to profit.
- Skipping insurance or licensing to start faster.
- Relying only on referrals or storm seasons, so the calendar empties in quiet months. See roofing marketing in the off-season (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-marketing-off-season).
- Slow follow-up. Homeowners book whoever responds first. See how to follow up on roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-lead-follow-up).
- Buying shared leads that five other roofers are also calling. See shared vs exclusive roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/shared-vs-exclusive-roofing-leads).

### When you are ready to grow
Once the basics work, growth comes from a predictable flow of leads, fast follow-up and a sales process your team can repeat. Our system is built for roofing companies doing $1M+ a year; read how to grow a roofing business (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-to-grow-a-roofing-business) for the next stage.

### FAQ
Q: Do I need a license to start a roofing company?
A: Rules differ by state and sometimes by city. Check your state's contractor licensing board before you take any job.
Q: What insurance does a roofing company need?
A: General liability and workers compensation are the basics homeowners, contractors and suppliers usually ask about. A commercial insurance agent can tell you what your state and jobs require.
Q: How do new roofing companies get customers?
A: Usually from people who already know them, a strong Google Business Profile, local partners and paid ads that reach homeowners in their service area.
Q: How much do roofing leads cost for a new company?
A: It depends on market and offer. Our published roofing campaigns ranged from $3.75 to $24 per lead.
Q: Should I start with residential or commercial roofing?
A: Most new roofing companies start with residential repair and replacement, which needs less equipment and has shorter sales cycles. Commercial work usually comes later.

## How to Grow a Roofing Business: 8 Steps From Referrals to a Predictable Pipeline
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/how-to-grow-a-roofing-business

Short answer: To grow a roofing business, build a lead source you control instead of relying on referrals and storms, respond to every lead within minutes, use a repeatable sales process, track cost per signed job by source, and add crews and cash reserves before you scale ad spend.

Most roofing companies grow to a point on referrals and storm work, then stall. Getting past that point takes a predictable source of leads, follow-up that never lets a lead go cold, a sales process your team can repeat and the crews and cash to deliver. Here are the steps, with real numbers from roofing campaigns we have run.

### 8 steps to grow a roofing business
1. Know your numbers. Average job value, close rate, cost per lead and cost per signed job by source. You cannot scale what you do not measure.
2. Build a lead source you control. Referrals and storms are great but unpredictable. Paid campaigns under your own brand bring a steady flow. A Dallas roofer closed $127,500 and 34 installs in about 60 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/dallas-roofer-127500-closed-34-installs) with this kind of system.

4. Make sales repeatable. A clear inspection, presentation and follow-up process that every rep follows. See roofing sales training (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-sales-training).
5. Add replacement and financing offers. Bigger tickets and offers that answer the cost objection.
6. Keep the calendar full in quiet months. Old estimates, reviews, referrals and replacement campaigns. See roofing marketing in the off-season (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-marketing-off-season).
7. Grow crews before you grow ads. More leads than you can serve wastes money and damages reviews.
8. Protect cash flow. Roofing jobs are often paid on completion. Keep reserves before scaling spend.

## Roofing Sales Training: 7 Skills That Close More Roofing Jobs
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-sales-training

Short answer: Good roofing sales training teaches reps to respond within minutes, book the inspection on the first call, inspect thoroughly with photos, present clear options with financing, handle price objections with value, and follow up for weeks until the homeowner decides. Most lost roofing jobs are lost on speed and follow-up, not price.

Most roofing companies do not lose jobs on price. They lose them on speed, trust and follow-up. This roofing sales training covers the skills that move a homeowner from first contact to a signed contract, in the order they happen.

### The 7 roofing sales skills
1. Speed to lead. Call new leads within minutes. A homeowner who waits an hour has often booked someone else. Automate the first text so nobody waits. See how to follow up on roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-lead-follow-up).
2. Book the inspection on the first call. Offer two specific times instead of asking when works.
3. Build trust before the roof. Arrive on time, introduce yourself, explain what you will check and how long it takes.
4. Inspect and document. Take clear photos of every issue and show them to the homeowner. Photos turn a quote into a shared understanding.
5. Present options. Good, better and best, with what each includes and the warranty. Homeowners like to choose.
6. Offer financing. For replacements, a clear payment option answers the biggest objection. A $0-down, 0%-for-12-months offer produced 686 leads in 8 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/texas-roofer-686-leads-8-days-0-down-offer) for a Texas roofer. Financing offers need the lender's terms and disclosures.
7. Follow up until they decide. Many homeowners collect several quotes. A short, helpful follow-up sequence keeps you in front of them.

### Handling the price objection
When a homeowner says another quote was cheaper, ask what was included. Compare materials, underlayment, ventilation, warranty, cleanup and who does the work. Show your photos again. Many homeowners choose the roofer who explained the most, not the cheapest one.

### Sales training starts with better leads
No training fixes fake numbers or leads shared with five other roofers. Exclusive, phone-verified leads give your reps real conversations to practice on. See verified roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/verified-roofing-leads) and roofing CRM automation (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-crm-automation) for the system that gets leads to your reps in minutes.

### What to measure
- Time from lead to first contact.
- Contact rate: how many leads your team actually reaches.
- Inspection booking rate.
- Close rate by rep and by lead source.
- Average job value.

### Learn from roofing companies that are scaling
We share what is working in real roofing campaigns, from offers to follow-up, in our free roofing business mastermind (https://www.roofingsystems.co/privatemastermind) recording. Results from those campaigns are in our case studies (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies).

### FAQ
Q: What should roofing sales training cover?
A: Speed to lead, booking the inspection, building trust, documenting the inspection with photos, presenting options, financing and follow-up.
Q: How fast should a roofing rep call a new lead?
A: Within minutes. Homeowners often book the first roofer who responds, so automate the first text and call as soon as you can.
Q: How do roofing reps handle price objections?
A: By comparing what each quote includes, such as materials, ventilation, warranty and cleanup, and showing inspection photos that explain the work.
Q: Does financing help close roofing jobs?
A: For replacements it often does, because cost is the biggest objection. Financing offers need the lender's terms and required disclosures.

## 15 Roofing Marketing Ideas and Strategies That Bring In Jobs

Short answer: The roofing marketing strategies that work best combine a strong Google Business Profile and reviews, referrals and local partners, a fast website with a page for every service, paid ads with a specific offer, and fast follow-up on every lead, including old estimates. 2. Retarget website visitors. Remind people who looked but did not call, with financing and warranty ads.
3. Follow up on old estimates. Homeowners who got a quote and never signed are your warmest list.
4. Respond in minutes. The best marketing is wasted if leads wait hours. See roofing CRM automation (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-crm-automation).

### Turning ideas into a roofing marketing strategy
Pick a few ideas you can run every week, track which ones produce signed jobs, and put more into those. Paid ads bring volume quickly; reviews, referrals and SEO lower your cost over time. A: Reviews after every job, a referral program, a complete Google Business Profile, a page for every service, local partners, paid ads with a specific offer, retargeting and follow-up on old estimates.
Q: What is a good roofing marketing strategy?
A: Combine a few channels you can run every week, respond to leads in minutes, and measure each channel by cost per signed job.

A: Paid ads with a clear offer usually bring leads fastest. Reviews, referrals and SEO build more slowly but lower costs over time.

## Free Roofing Leads: 9 Honest Ways to Get Them, and When to Pay Instead
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/free-roofing-leads

Short answer: Free roofing leads come from referrals, reviews, a complete Google Business Profile, local partners, neighbor marketing, old estimates and helpful content. They cost time rather than money and grow slowly, so most growing roofing companies pair them with a paid lead source they control.

There is no list of free roofing leads waiting to be downloaded. But there are free ways to get homeowners to call you. They cost time instead of money, they grow slowly, and they work best alongside a paid source you control. Here are the ones that work.

### 9 ways to get free roofing leads
1. Referrals from past customers. Ask at the end of every job and thank people who refer.
2. Google reviews. Send the review link the same day the job is done.
3. Google Business Profile. Complete categories, service areas and real job photos. See roofing SEO (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-seo).
4. Neighbor marketing. Yard signs and a note to neighbors when you finish a roof.
5. Old estimates. Homeowners who got a quote and never signed. A seasonal follow-up costs nothing.
6. Real estate agents and home inspectors. They see roofs that need work before a sale.
7. Property managers. A source of repair and commercial work. See commercial roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/commercial-roofing-leads).
8. Helpful content. Answer the questions homeowners search for on your website.
9. Community presence. Local groups, events and sponsorships where homeowners already gather.

### The limits of free roofing leads
Free channels are worth building, but they are slow and hard to scale on demand. You cannot turn on more referrals the week your crews are free. That is why most roofing companies past their first year add a paid source they control.

### Free vs paid roofing leads

Source | Cost | Speed | Control
Referrals and reviews | Free (time) | Slow | Low

### FAQ

A: Yes, through referrals, reviews, a complete Google Business Profile, local partners, neighbor marketing and old estimates. They cost time instead of money and grow slowly.
Q: What is the best free source of roofing leads?
A: For most roofers, referrals and reviews from past customers, because those homeowners already trust you.
Q: Are free roofing lead lists real?
A: Be careful. Downloaded lists of homeowners are not people asking for a roofer. Real leads are homeowners who contacted you or asked for a quote.
Q: When should a roofer pay for leads?
A: When free channels cannot fill the calendar on demand. A paid source you control lets you add leads when your crews have capacity.

## How to Get Roofing Leads From Insurance Companies (and What Actually Works)
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-leads-from-insurance-companies

Short answer: Insurance companies rarely send leads directly to roofers. Insurance-related roofing work usually comes from homeowners after a storm, so roofers get it through storm campaigns, a strong local reputation, relationships with local insurance agents and contractor networks some carriers use, and by helping homeowners through inspections without promising claim outcomes.

Insurance companies do not usually hand roofing leads to contractors. But a lot of roofing work involves an insurance claim, and there are honest ways to be the roofer homeowners call when it does. This guide explains how insurance-related roofing work comes in, the relationships that help and the rules to respect.

### How insurance-related roofing work really comes in
After hail or wind, homeowners check their roofs, file claims and look for a roofer. The insurer pays according to the policy, but the homeowner usually chooses who does the work. So the real question is how to be the roofer that homeowner trusts and finds first.

### 6 honest ways to get insurance-related roofing leads
1. Run storm campaigns in affected areas. Target the ZIP codes hit by a storm with an inspection offer. See storm damage leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/storm-damage-leads).
2. Build relationships with local insurance agents. Independent agents get asked by their clients which roofer to call. Be the one they trust.
3. Learn about contractor networks. Some carriers and claims programs work with approved contractor networks. Requirements and availability vary by carrier and state.
4. Know the claims process. Homeowners value a roofer who documents damage with clear photos and explains the inspection and claims steps.
5. Get reviews that mention storm work. Homeowners after a storm look for a local, established company, not a storm chaser.
6. Follow up for weeks. Claims take time. Keep in touch until the homeowner is ready.

### Rules to respect
- Do not promise a claim outcome. Only the insurer decides what is covered.
- Rules on contractors and claims differ by state. Some states restrict what contractors can say or offer about deductibles and claims. Check your state's rules before you advertise.
- Keep your license and insurance current, and show them. Homeowners and agents check.

### When the next storm hits
A campaign that is ready before storm season can launch within hours in affected areas, with phone verification and instant follow-up. See storm damage leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/storm-damage-leads), our seasonal notes for Texas (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-leads-texas) and Florida (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-leads-florida), and how to follow up on roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-lead-follow-up).

### FAQ
Q: Do insurance companies give roofing leads?
A: Rarely directly. Homeowners usually choose their own roofer after filing a claim, so roofers win this work through storm campaigns, local reputation and relationships with insurance agents.
Q: How do roofers work with insurance agents?
A: By building trust with local independent agents, whose clients often ask which roofer to call after a storm.
Q: Can a roofer promise the insurance will pay?
A: No. Only the insurer decides what is covered. Roofers can document damage and explain the inspection and claims steps.
Q: Are there rules for insurance roofing work?
A: Yes, and they differ by state. Some states restrict what contractors can offer or say about deductibles and claims, so check your state's rules before advertising.

## 12 Roofing Advertising Ideas That Get Homeowners to Call
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-advertising-ideas

Short answer: The roofing advertising ideas that work best lead with a specific offer (such as financing), use real job footage instead of stock photos, build on your reviews, and send every click to a matching landing page with fast follow-up.

Most roofing ads look the same: a stock photo and "free inspection". These ideas are built to stand out, and several come straight from campaigns we've run, with the numbers linked.

### Offer ideas
1. Financing offers. A $0-down, 0%-for-12-months offer took a Texas roofer from zero leads to 686 in 8 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/texas-roofer-686-leads-8-days-0-down-offer). Financing offers need the lender's terms and required disclosures.
2. Answer the fear, not the feature. Speak to what worries homeowners (cost, mess, being upsold) instead of listing roofing materials.
3. A specific inspection promise. Replace "free inspection" with something concrete, such as a photo report of the roof sent the same day.

### Creative ideas
1. Owner-to-camera video. A short vertical video of the owner explaining the offer builds trust fast.
2. Before and after. Drone shots of the old and new roof on the same house.
3. Crew at work. Real crews on real roofs beat stock photos every time.
4. Review-led ads. In Dallas (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/dallas-roofer-127500-closed-34-installs), ads built around the company's Google reviews and local reputation led to $127,500 closed and 34 installs.
5. Test several angles. Run multiple creatives and keep only the ones that hold a click-through rate above 2%, as most of our lowest-cost campaigns did. More in roofing ads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-ad-creatives).

### Channel and timing ideas
1. Instagram Reels and Stories. Vertical video placements inside your Meta campaigns: Instagram ads for roofers (https://www.roofingsystems.co/instagram-ads-for-roofers).
2. Storm-response campaigns. Prepared creative that launches within hours after hail or wind in your service area: storm damage leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/storm-damage-leads).
3. Retargeting. Show follow-up ads to homeowners who watched your video or visited your page but didn't book.
4. Neighborhood targeting around jobs. Advertise to the streets around a current job while the crew is there.
Every idea needs a landing page and follow-up: Great ads fail when the click lands on a slow homepage or the lead waits hours for a call. Pair ads with roofing landing pages (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-landing-pages) and automated follow-up (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-crm-automation).

### FAQ
Q: What is the best way to advertise a roofing company?
A: Lead with a specific offer, use real job footage and reviews, run ads on Meta or Google under your own brand, and send clicks to a matching landing page with fast follow-up.
Q: Do financing offers work in roofing ads?
A: They can. In our Texas campaign a $0-down, 0%-for-12-months offer produced 686 homeowner leads in 8 days. Financing offers require the lender's terms and disclosures.
Q: Should roofing ads use video?
A: Yes, short vertical video works well on Instagram Reels, Facebook and TikTok. Real crews, before-and-after footage and owner-to-camera clips perform better than stock imagery.
Q: How do I know if a roofing ad is working?
A: Track click-through rate, cost per lead and, most importantly, cost per booked inspection and signed job.

## Shared vs. Exclusive Roofing Leads: What You're Really Paying For
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/shared-vs-exclusive-roofing-leads

Short answer: Shared leads are sold to several roofers at once; exclusive leads are sold to one. Both are rented from a lead seller. An owned lead generation system is the third option: homeowners respond to your brand directly and the pages, CRM and data stay with you.

Every roofing company that grows past referrals ends up asking the same question: should we buy leads, or build our own way of getting them? Here is a plain comparison of shared leads, exclusive leads and an owned lead generation system: what each one actually gives you, and where each one breaks.

### The three options, defined
- Shared leads: a lead seller captures a homeowner's request and sells the same contact to several roofing companies. Whoever calls first usually has the advantage.
- Exclusive leads: the lead seller sells each contact to one company only. You pay more per lead, but you are not racing other roofers for the same homeowner.
- An owned system: you (or a partner working under your brand) run the ads, landing pages, CRM and follow-up. Homeowners respond directly to your company, and the assets stay with you.

### Shared leads: fast, cheap per lead, crowded
Shared leads are easy to start: sign up, set a service area, and contacts arrive. The trade-off is competition. The homeowner often hears from several roofers within minutes, so the conversation tends to become about who answered first and who is cheapest, not who is the best fit.
- Good for: filling gaps quickly, testing a new service area.
- Watch out for: paying for contacts who never answer, price-driven buyers, and a pipeline that disappears when you stop paying.

### Exclusive leads: less competition, still rented
Exclusive leads remove the race against other contractors for that contact, which usually makes conversations easier. But you still do not control how the lead was generated, what the homeowner was promised, or how qualified they are, and the flow still belongs to the seller.
- Good for: roofers who want more predictable conversations without building marketing in-house.
- Watch out for: vague definitions of "exclusive" and "qualified". Read the contract terms on refunds and replacements before you sign.

### An owned system: slower to set up, compounds over time
With your own system, the ads run under your name, the landing pages make your offer, and every lead goes into your CRM with your follow-up. It takes setup (offer, creatives, pages, automations), but each piece keeps working and improving, and the customer data is yours.
For a sense of scale: one Texas roofer went from zero leads to 686 homeowner inquiries in 8 days (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/texas-roofer-686-leads-8-days-0-down-offer) once an owned system with a clear offer was running, and another generated 825 verified leads at $4.95 each (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/825-verified-roofing-leads-4-95-cpl) in five weeks.
- Good for: established roofing companies (we work with $1M+ roofers) that want predictable growth they control.
- Watch out for: doing it in pieces. Ads from one vendor, a website from another and follow-up in a third tool is where most owned setups break down.

### Side-by-side comparison
- Competition for the homeowner: high for shared leads, low for exclusive leads, none for an owned system (they responded to your brand).
- Control over the message and offer: none with shared or exclusive leads, full with an owned system.
- Qualification: with shared and exclusive leads it depends on the seller; with an owned system you set the rules.
- What you keep if you stop paying: nothing with shared or exclusive leads; with an owned system you keep the pages, CRM, audiences, creatives and customer data.
- Setup effort: minimal for shared and exclusive leads, significant for an owned system unless a partner installs it.

### How to choose
If you need appointments next week and have no marketing in place, bought leads can bridge the gap. If you are an established roofing company planning for the next few years, the question is less "what does a lead cost" and more "what does a booked, qualified inspection cost, and do I own the machine that produces it?"
Whichever route you take, speed matters: a lead that waits is a lead someone else answers. Read how to follow up on roofing leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-lead-follow-up) for a follow-up process you can apply to any lead source.
How we approach it: We install the owned option for $1M+ roofing companies: offer, Facebook and Instagram ads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/facebook-ads-for-roofers), landing pages, CRM, AI follow-up and qualification, as one system. More on the roofing lead generation system (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-lead-generation).

### FAQ
Q: What is the difference between shared and exclusive roofing leads?
A: A shared lead is sold to several roofing companies at once, so you compete for the same homeowner. An exclusive lead is sold to only one company. Both are bought from a lead seller, so neither gives you ownership of the marketing that produced them.
Q: Are exclusive roofing leads worth the higher price?
A: They can be, because you are not racing other contractors for the same contact. Check how the seller defines exclusive and qualified, and what happens with bad or unreachable leads, before signing.
Q: What is the alternative to buying roofing leads?
A: Running your own lead generation: ads under your brand, your own landing pages, a CRM and a follow-up process. It takes more setup, but the homeowners respond directly to you and the assets stay with your company.

## How to Follow Up on Roofing Leads (and Book More Inspections)
URL: https://www.roofingsystems.co/blog/roofing-lead-follow-up

Short answer: Respond to every roofing lead within minutes with an automatic text and email, call as soon as possible, qualify before driving out, book the inspection on the first conversation, and keep following up by call, text and email until the homeowner books or says no.

Most roofing leads are not lost to a competitor's better price. They are lost to silence. The homeowner fills in a form, waits, gets busy, and books with whoever reached them first. Here is a follow-up process you can run on every lead, whatever the source.

### 1. Respond immediately, every time
The first response should happen within minutes, not at the end of the day. A homeowner who just asked about a roof is thinking about it right now; an hour later they are back at work, and the next roofer who calls gets the conversation.
- Send an automatic text and email the moment a lead arrives, confirming you received the request and saying when someone will call.
- Call as soon as possible after that. If nobody answers, leave a short voicemail and follow with a text.
- Route new leads to whoever is available, rather than to one person's inbox.

### 2. Qualify before you drive out
An inspection costs your team time and fuel. A few questions up front protect that time and make the appointment more useful for the homeowner:
- Do they own the home, and is the property inside your service area?
- What prompted the request: a leak, storm damage, an older roof, selling the home?
- Is there an insurance claim involved, or is it a retail job?
- Who else needs to be at the appointment to make a decision?
- What timeline are they working to?

### 3. Book the inspection on the first conversation
Offer two or three specific time slots instead of asking "when works for you?". Confirm by text straight away, and send a reminder the day before and on the morning of the appointment. Make rescheduling easy: a homeowner who can move the appointment is less likely to simply not show up.

### 4. Keep following up after no answer
Many leads go quiet rather than say no. One unanswered call is not a decision. Set up a sequence that mixes calls, texts and emails over the following days and weeks, and stop only when the homeowner books, says no, or asks you to stop.
1. Day 1: instant text and email, first call, voicemail and follow-up text if unanswered.
2. Days 2–3: another call at a different time of day, plus a short helpful text (for example, what to expect at an inspection).
3. First week: an email with useful information: photos of common roof issues, how insurance inspections work in your area, your warranty.
4. Following weeks: a lighter-touch check-in by text or email until the homeowner responds.
Keep it helpful: Follow-up works when each message gives the homeowner something useful or makes the next step easier. Ten messages of "just checking in" will be ignored; a reminder about a storm-damage inspection window will not.

### 5. Follow up after the estimate, too
Homeowners often collect several estimates before choosing. The roofer who follows up clearly (answering questions, explaining the scope, making it easy to say yes) is often the one who wins, even without the lowest price. Put post-estimate follow-up in the same system so it never depends on someone remembering.

### 6. Track everything in a CRM
If follow-up lives in someone's head or a notebook, it will slip in busy weeks, exactly when you have the most leads. A CRM shows every lead's status, who contacted them and when, and which leads need action today. It also tells you which lead sources produce booked jobs, not just form fills.
Real example: In a 16-day Florida campaign across 4 locations, every one of 365 OTP-verified leads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/case-studies/florida-365-otp-verified-leads-4-locations) was synced instantly to the CRM, nurtured by SMS and email, and routed to sales: follow-up running automatically, not from memory.

### Automating the process
Most of the steps above can run automatically: instant replies, reminders, follow-up sequences and pipeline updates. Your team then spends its time on the conversations that need a person. In the system we install for $1M+ roofers, every lead from our Facebook and Instagram ads (https://www.roofingsystems.co/facebook-ads-for-roofers) goes into a CRM with AI follow-up, email and SMS sequences and qualification. See the full roofing lead generation system (https://www.roofingsystems.co/roofing-lead-generation).

### FAQ
Q: How fast should I respond to a roofing lead?
A: Within minutes. Send an automatic text and email immediately, then call as soon as possible. The longer a lead waits, the more likely the homeowner has spoken to another roofer or moved on.
Q: How many times should I follow up with a roofing lead?
A: Keep following up with a mix of calls, texts and emails until the homeowner books, says no, or asks you to stop. Many leads go quiet rather than decline, so a single unanswered call is not a decision.
Q: Should roofers use a CRM for follow-up?
A: Yes. A CRM keeps every lead's status and history in one place, makes sure nothing is missed in busy weeks, and shows which lead sources turn into booked jobs.
